title: Lesson 78: Org Governance: Change Management, Release Calendars, and the DevOps Culture Behind Both
description: Decision rights, change tiers, the fixed Salesforce release calendar, release windows sized against real intake, and the DevOps norms that keep a governance model from being routed around.

questions.question: A release manager has 90 change requests for the quarter and 13 production windows that each handle 4 changes. The team responds by bundling unrelated work into single change sets and by declaring more requests urgent. Per the lesson, what is the actual defect and the correct first move?
options: The team is not working enough weekends. Add a second Saturday window and require overtime sign-off.
Validation and deployment are too slow. Automate them and the 38-change shortfall closes.
Two risk classes are sharing one pipe. Classify the low-risk reports and permission work into a separate, more frequent lane so the heavy window is no longer overloaded.
The intake queue is the problem. Ask the business to submit fewer requests until the backlog clears.
questions.explanation: Fifty-two slots against 90 requests leaves 38 changes unshippable per quarter. The lesson's worked example shows the shortfall closes when standard-tier work moves to a weekly lane, leaving 30 heavy changes across 13 windows against a capacity of 4. Faster validation does not fix a constraint that is window frequency and classification.

questions.question: An architect is defending a production change policy that says any failed release will be rolled back to the previous state. The team deploys with change sets. What must the architect change about that promise?
options: Nothing. A failed change set deployment rolls back the whole transaction automatically.

A successful change set deployment cannot be rolled back and change sets cannot delete or rename components, so recovery means a forward fix or a separately deployed previous metadata state, and the review gate has to carry more weight.
Change sets can be recalled after upload, so rollback is available as long as the architect acts within the same day.
Rollback is available only when the target is a sandbox, so production policy should reference the sandbox procedure.
questions.explanation: Change set deployment is a one-way transaction: if it fails partway the transaction rolls back, but once it succeeds the changes are committed. Combined with the inability to delete or rename components and the ban on recalling an uploaded change set, the policy has to be rewritten around validation and forward repair.

questions.question: Emergency changes are 28 percent of a client's production changes, and the CAB responds by requiring more approvals on the emergency path. Why does the lesson call that the wrong fix?
options: Emergency volume is unrelated to process design and should be tracked only for audit purposes.
A high emergency share means the normal path is too slow or unpredictable, so tightening the emergency path leaves the cause in place and pushes teams to bypass governance another way.
Emergencies should be blocked entirely, because production defects never justify an unplanned change.
The right fix is to remove the emergency tier and route every change through the major tier for consistency.
questions.explanation: The lesson treats emergency inflation as a process defect: teams declare emergencies because waiting on the normal path costs more. The fix is to measure normal lead time, find the waiting, and shorten the normal path, not to add friction to the only route that currently works.
